newsitem.title: INDIA: India eyes Iraq crude, sells tea in U.N. deal.
newsitem.headline: India eyes Iraq crude, sells tea in U.N. deal.

text.p: India, responding to a U.N.-supervised oil-for-food programme, signalled on Friday that it could import up to one million tonnes of crude from Iraq and sell tea to the Middle Eastern country.

A senior Petroleum Ministry official said the ministry had permitted state-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) to import up to one million tonnes of crude oil from Iraq in the second phase of the United Nations programme.

"Once the United Nations permits the second sale of crude oil under the oil-for-food programme, a delegation comprising IOC and ministry officials would head for Iraq to contract the purchase," the official told Reuters.
The actual quantity contracted from Iraq and the price per barrel would depend on what the U.N. permitted, he said.
Earlier on Friday India's Tea Board said in Calcutta that Tata Tea had secured permission to export 1,000 tonnes of black tea to Iraq under the oil-for-food programme.
A statement from the state-run Tea Board said Tata Tea had secured an order to ship 1,000 tonnes of tea, which the company is expected to export in the "immediate future".
The statement did not say how much Iraqi crude oil India would receive as part of the deal.

"There is no direct exchange with crude," Tea Board chairman S.S. Ahuja said. "Iraq's earning from selling crude is kept in banks under U.N. supervision and in exchange for that letters of credit are issued to import food items including tea."

During 1996/97 (April-March), the government allowed IOC to import up to 500,000 tonnes of Iraqi crude under the first phase of the $2.0 billion oil-for-food programme, but the contracted volume was lower because India was a late entrant in the negotiations, the Petroleum Ministry official said.
An official of the government's Oil Coordination Committee said the volume supplied last year was 50,000 tonnes at a price of $19 per barrel.

The official said the new oil-for-food package with Iraq had yet to be completed since Iraq was still negotiating with the U.N. to relax some conditions. The U.N. imposed economic sanctions on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Iraq is expected to more than double its oil exports next month to around 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) to make up for a gap between the end of the first oil-for-food deal and the beginning of the second.

The second deal began on June 8 but Iraq has delayed exporting oil for two months and will now have to sell oil at a much higher rate in August than previously reckoned, or forego some of its oil sales under the scheme.
The U.N. confirmed on Wednesday that Iraq must sell around $1 billion worth of oil by early September under the renewed oil-for-food deal.
